query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Tailored thermo‐mechanical processing (i.e., a controlled sequence of severe plastic deformation via rolling followed by precise annealing) will refine the as‐cast eutectic high-entropy alloy into an ultrafine duplex microstructure with inherited lamellar features that simultaneously increases strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with a conventional, coarser eutectic microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a single intervention consisting of rolling (severe plastic deformation) followed by a controlled annealing treatment to induce microstructural refinement.
generation.conditions: The intervention is to be carried out under conditions where the rolling intensity and annealing temperature/time are optimized to promote phase decomposition and the formation of a hierarchically duplex lamellar structure; experiments should be performed at room temperature under uniaxial tension.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine duplex microstructure featuring inherited lamellar architecture that provides a two-hierarchical constraint effect and activates self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: The processing-induced microstructure increases the density of interfaces and grain boundaries that impede dislocation movement (strengthening effect) while the lamellar architecture allows for controlled plasticity and crack arresting (improving ductility).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the processed alloy will exhibit a statistically significant increase in both yield strength and ductility. Although exact improvements depend on optimization, improvements on the order of tens of percentage points (e.g., 20-30% increase in yield strength and a similar relative improvement in ductility) are anticipated.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy without any tailored thermo-mechanical processing.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for eutectic high-entropy alloys with similar composition and casting conditions; deviations in composition, cooling rates, or processing limits may affect the establishment of the desired duplex microstructure and the resulting mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantitative improvements are uncertain without further optimization studies, and the effectiveness of the intervention could depend sensitively on processing parameters (e.g., degree of deformation, annealing temperature/time).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical eutectic high-entropy alloy samples. Process one set using standard casting (baseline) and the other using the proposed tailored thermo-mechanical processing. Characterize microstructures using SEM/TEM to confirm the formation of the ultrafine duplex lamellar structure. Perform uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature to measure yield strength and ductility. Use statistical analysis to compare results between the two sets.
measurements: Grain size and lamellae spacing (using electron microscopy)
Phase distribution and presence of duplex microstructure (using XRD/EBSD)
Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation at fracture (tensile testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the thermo-mechanically processed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in both yield strength and ductility compared to the as-cast baseline, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the formation of an ultrafine duplex lamellar architecture.

cited_evidence.text:
Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism.
